entry.title: Small Findings
entry.summary: Short notes from side projects. Each one is something I measured or hit, not a general claim.
entry.content:
Short notes from side projects. Each one is something I measured or hit, not a general claim.

Godot 4.8 beta 2 makes my Android APK about 6 MB smaller

2026-11-02

Salt Line, my Rust + Godot artillery game, ships on Godot 4.7.2. I keep an opt-in CI job that exports the same project with both 4.7.2 and 4.8-beta2 and compares the results.

Both exports below use Godot's official export templates, for arm64 Android, with release builds. My shipping 4.7.2 build uses a stripped custom engine instead, so these aren't my store sizes. They do compare like with like.

4.7.24.8-beta2Change
Salt Line APK90,869,703 B84,594,405 B−6,275,298 B (−6.9%)
libgodot_android.so in the APK71,114,944 B64,818,536 B−6,296,408 B (−8.9%)
libsalt_line_godot.so (my Rust GDExtension) in the APK6,077,720 B6,077,720 B0 B

Almost all of the drop is the engine library. My own native library is byte-for-byte the same size. So the savings come from Godot, not from anything I changed.

Not everything got smaller. The Linux x86_64 release export grew by 3,135,744 B (78.6 MB → 81.7 MB), the same amount as the official Linux template grew. I haven't looked into what changed in the engine on either platform.

The numbers come from one CI run (41565869845) against 4.8-beta2 commit cafc17a19. Betas change, so I'll measure again at the release candidate.

The export that didn't build at first

The first 4.8 Android export failed in Gradle:

GodotApp.java:49: error: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   variable FLAVOR
  location: class BuildConfig

4.8 moved com/godot/game/GodotApp.java to com/godot/game/app/GodotApplication.java. My build script unpacked the 4.8 Android build template over the 4.7.2 one that the job had just used, so the old GodotApp.java stayed behind and was compiled against 4.8's Gradle project.

The fix was to delete android/build before unpacking the template (saltline#144). If you switch Godot versions in one checkout and see a strange Java error in the Android export, check for files left over from the old template.

Godot 4.8: vulkan=false is no longer enough for a Vulkan-less build

2026-11-12

I ship Salt Line with a stripped Godot engine, compiled from a build profile that turns off what the game doesn't use, Vulkan included. On Godot 4.7.2 that profile sets "vulkan": false. When I built the same profile against 4.8-beta3, the Android template stopped compiling:

platform/android/display_server_android.cpp:883:2: error: use of undeclared identifier 'free_vulkan_global_context'

The cause is a new option in 4.8. SConstruct now has a rendering_device option, on by default, and defines RD_ENABLED from it. In 4.7.2, only the Vulkan driver turned on RD_ENABLED on Android. So vulkan=false now leaves RD_ENABLED defined without VULKAN_ENABLED. The Android display server's destructor calls free_vulkan_global_context() under #if defined(RD_ENABLED), but the header only declares that function under #ifdef VULKAN_ENABLED.

The fix is to turn off the new option as well:

"vulkan": false,
"rendering_device": false

That's also the setting you want: with no Vulkan driver there's nothing for RenderingDevice to drive. You can't put it in a profile you still use for 4.7.2, though, because 4.7.2 doesn't have the option. My trial build adds it on top of the 4.7.2 profile and checks that every option it sets exists in the Godot tree it builds (saltline#154).

With that change, the stripped 4.8-beta3 arm64 libgodot_android.so is 21,041,224 B, against 23,186,048 B for my shipping 4.7.2 engine. That's 2.1 MB (9%) smaller, before I've tried turning off the new tilemap and texture_streaming modules.

The same code is on beta2 and on Godot's master, so this isn't a beta3 regression. I only hit it now because beta2's trial never built the stripped engine. If you build a Vulkan-less Godot 4.8, set rendering_device=false too.

entry.title: Fixing a Black HDMI Picture on My LG C2 After Installing CleanYourTV
entry.summary: I customized my downstairs LG C2 with CleanYourTV. The next morning, my Apple TV would turn on, but selecting its HDMI input left me staring at a black screen.
entry.content:
I customized my downstairs LG C2 with CleanYourTV. The next morning, my Apple TV would turn on, but selecting its HDMI input left me staring at a black screen.

The TV could see the Apple TV. It could see a video signal. It still wasn't putting that video on the screen.

Here's what I checked over SSH, what restored the picture, and the boot workaround I installed afterward.

Update: The boot workaround has held through a cold boot. I also went back and traced the stale subscription live, and tried to bring back the black screen without the workaround. See Tracing the stale subscription for what that did and didn't prove.

The Setup

  • LG C2, model OLED77C2AUA
  • Firmware 33.31.68
  • webOS SDK 10.3.1
  • CleanYourTV replacing LG's Home launcher
  • Apple TV connected to HDMI 1
  • Existing root SSH access to the TV

These details matter. This is a report from one TV and one firmware combination, not a fix for every LG black screen.

CleanYourTV customizes a rooted webOS TV. Its Home takeover uses writable files and temporary mounts, and on the configuration installed on my TV, it restarts LG's system app manager, SAM. The project's TV changes documentation explains the boot setup. Check your installed scripts too; upstream code can change.

First, Wake the Apple TV

The first SSH check said the Apple TV was connected, but its CEC power state was Off and there was no HDMI signal.

Pressing Home on the Apple TV remote changed that:

{
  "hdmiPlugIn": true,
  "hdmiSignalExist": true,
  "cecPower": "On"
}

So a sleeping Apple TV wasn't the problem, or at least not all of it. The screen was still black.

Check More Than the Selected Input

The following commands run on the TV, after logging in through your existing root SSH connection. The </dev/null redirect keeps luna-send from waiting on SSH's standard input.

# Connected devices and HDMI signal state
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.eim/getAllInputStatus '{}' </dev/null

# Which app LG considers foreground
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/getForegroundAppInfo '{}' </dev/null

# Media pipelines and their foreground state
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.media/getActivePipelines '{}' </dev/null

# What is actually connected to the display's video output
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.videooutput/getStatus '{}' </dev/null

# Mute state for each media context
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.avmutemanager/getMuteInfo '{}' </dev/null

The results disagreed with each other:

CheckBefore recoveryAfter recovery
Apple TV powerOnOn
HDMI 1 signalPresentPresent
Foreground appcom.webos.app.hdmi1com.webos.app.hdmi1
HDMI media pipelinesNot foregroundForeground
Main video outputDisconnected, no source assignedHDMI 1, 3840 × 2160, 60 Hz, Dolby Vision
HDMI picture muteActiveUnmuted (current context)

The selected input wasn't the whole story. LG's app manager considered HDMI 1 foreground, but the media service still treated its pipelines as background sessions, and the video output had nothing routed to its main display sink.

The Recovery That Worked

I restarted the media service and reopened HDMI 1. Substitute the correct HDMI app if your source uses another port.

systemctl restart umediaserver
sleep 3

luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/closeByAppId \
  '{"id":"com.webos.app.hdmi1"}' </dev/null

sleep 2

luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/launch \
  '{"id":"com.webos.app.hdmi1"}' </dev/null

This interrupts media playback. It doesn't reset the TV or erase its settings.

Afterward, the main output was connected to HDMI 1 at 3840 × 2160, 60 Hz, Dolby Vision. The media pipelines became foreground sessions, and the mute manager reported the current session's picture and audio unmuted.

I checked the screen. Apple TV was back.

One diagnostic gotcha: videooutput/getStatus still showed its own muted flag as true. Older media contexts also remained in the mute manager's list. Match mute information to the current output context, and confirm the picture on the TV. One boolean isn't enough.

What Happened

The CleanYourTV boot log (/tmp/cleanyourtv-boot.log, timestamps in seconds since boot) showed:

24.37 home: mounting the launcher over LG's Home, restarting sam
24.67 home: sam restarted
25.68 after-sam: webOS SDK 10.3.1, Home 'com.webos.app.home flutter', services: none

Each process's start time is field 22 of /proc/<pid>/stat, in clock ticks since boot (100 per second here):

cut -d ' ' -f 1,2,22 /proc/$(pidof umediaserver)/stat /proc/$(pidof sam)/stat

2551 (umediaserver) 1022
3940 (sam) 2466

The media service started about 10.2 seconds after boot. SAM's current instance started at 24.66 seconds, matching the restart in the boot log. So the media service was the original process from before the SAM restart, still running more than an hour and a half later when I investigated. Restarting that service and reopening the input repaired the disagreement between app foreground state and media routing.

That matches what I saw: the media service never heard about the SAM restart, and it kept treating HDMI as background even after SAM brought HDMI 1 to the foreground.

Tracing the stale subscription

A week later I went back to find the specific subscription. ls-monitor -s lists every subscription on webOS's Luna bus, and ls-monitor -l maps bus names to processes. Inside umediaserver, a client called com.webos.media.appobserver subscribes to two SAM methods:

com.webos.applicationManager foregroundAppsEx  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"extraInfo":true, "subscribe":true}
com.webos.applicationManager getAppLifeStatus  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"subscribe":true}

foregroundAppsEx is how the media service learns which app is in the foreground. I briefly turned the workaround off, restarted only SAM, and listed subscriptions again:

com.webos.applicationManager getAppLifeStatus  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"subscribe":true}

The app observer re-subscribed to getAppLifeStatus but never to foregroundAppsEx. A minute later it still hadn't. Restarting umediaserver brought both subscriptions back.

That is the stale subscription: after a SAM restart, the media service stops receiving foreground-app updates until it is restarted itself.

Trying to bring the black screen back

Next I tried to recreate the original failure with the workaround off. For each test I checked the media pipelines and the main video output over SSH, and looked at the screen:

TestforegroundAppsExHDMI 1 picture
Restart only SAM, reopen HDMI 1MissingFine
Reboot (same boot order as the incident: media service at 10.3 s, SAM restarted at 33.9 s), switch to HDMI 1MissingFine
From that boot: TV off with the LG remote, wake with the Apple TV remote over CECMissingFine

The stale subscription showed up every time, including on a real boot. The black screen never did. The last test is the closest match to the original morning: the TV sat in standby with a stale media service, and the Apple TV woke it. Standby doesn't restart webOS, so the same umediaserver process carried through.

So here's where it stands:

  • Proven: a SAM restart leaves umediaserver without its foregroundAppsEx subscription, and only restarting umediaserver restores it. Every CleanYourTV boot on this TV restarts SAM.
  • Proven: on the morning of the incident, restarting umediaserver and reopening HDMI 1 fixed a disconnected main output.
  • Not proven: that the missing subscription caused the black screen by itself. In my tests the TV handled HDMI without it, so something else was also involved that morning. A long standby, a particular CEC handshake, or a timing race are all possible, but I couldn't reproduce it on demand.

That also changes how to read the cold-boot result. HDMI came up fine with the workaround, but it came up fine without it too. I'm keeping the workaround anyway. It's cheap, it makes the stale subscription impossible, and it's the same restart that fixed the real failure. I've only seen this on SDK 10.3.1, and it doesn't mean every CleanYourTV installation is affected.

Preparing for the Next Boot

The installed CleanYourTV version already had an after-sam.sh hook. It asks tvprofile.js which running services need restarting after SAM.

On this TV, that decision returned an empty string. I changed the afterSam rule in /media/developer/cleanyourtv/tvprofile.js to return umediaserver for SDK 10.3.1 only:

// before
afterSam: (major > 0 && major < 7) || /\snative$/.test(homeKind) ? 'eim webapp-mgr preload-manager memorymanager' : '',

// after
afterSam: f.sdk === '10.3.1' ? 'umediaserver' : (major > 0 && major < 7) || /\snative$/.test(homeKind) ? 'eim webapp-mgr preload-manager memorymanager' : '',

Other SDK decisions and the existing legacy service rule stay intact. The existing boot hook then restarts the media service before opening Home. This changes a file under /media/developer/cleanyourtv, not the read-only firmware.

I saved the original profile first. Rolling back means restoring that copy; the rollback takes effect on the next boot.

The updated JavaScript passed a syntax check using the TV's own runtime, and the TV returned the expected boot decision.

Since then, the TV has cold-booted with the workaround in place and HDMI came up normally (though, as the tests above show, that alone doesn't prove the workaround is what prevents the failure). Restarting a shared media service can affect other boot media clients, so I kept the workaround specific to the SDK I observed.

A CleanYourTV update can replace the modified profile. After updating, check whether the upstream version addresses the issue before reapplying a local change.

What I'd Check Next Time

  1. Wake the source and verify there is an HDMI signal.
  2. Check the foreground app.
  3. Compare that with the media pipelines and main video output.
  4. If the signal is present but routing is disconnected, restart umediaserver and reopen the input (see above).
  5. Confirm the picture physically before calling it fixed.

I used Codex to collect the SSH diagnostics, work through the recovery, and prepare the local boot workaround. What cracked it was comparing what each service believed: the input was selected; the video just wasn't being routed to the screen.

entry.title: 5x Faster Shell Startup: A macOS Developer Environment Audit
entry.summary: My shell took 2.5 seconds to start. Now it takes 0.47 seconds. Here's what I learned.
entry.content:
My shell took 2.5 seconds to start. Now it takes 0.47 seconds. Here's what I learned.

The Problem

Every new terminal tab felt sluggish. I'd open a tab, wait, then forget what I was about to do. Death by a thousand cuts.

$ time zsh -i -c exit
zsh -i -c exit  0.31s user 0.53s system 33% cpu 2.509 total

2.5 seconds. For a shell prompt.

Finding the Culprits

The usual suspects in a developer's .zshrc:

ToolWhat it doesStartup cost
pyenvPython version manager~300ms
nvsNode version manager~200ms
SDKMANJava/Kotlin version manager~400ms
Google Cloud SDKgcloud CLI~200ms
Oh My ZshShell framework~100ms
Greeting scriptInspirational quotes~500ms

That's 1.7 seconds just from version managers I use maybe once a week.

The Fix: Lazy Loading

The insight: I don't need pyenv initialized until I actually run python. Same for Java, Node, and gcloud.

Before (eager loading)

# Every shell startup pays this cost
eval "$(pyenv init --path)"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"

[[ -s "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh" ]] && source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"

[ -s "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh" ] && . "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh"

After (lazy loading)

# pyenv - only initialize on first use
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"

_pyenv_init() {
  unfunction pyenv python python3 pip pip3 2>/dev/null
  eval "$(command pyenv init --path)"
  eval "$(command pyenv init -)"
}

pyenv() { _pyenv_init; pyenv "$@" }
python() { _pyenv_init; python "$@" }
python3() { _pyenv_init; python3 "$@" }
pip() { _pyenv_init; pip "$@" }
pip3() { _pyenv_init; pip3 "$@" }

The trick: create shell functions that shadow the real commands. On first invocation, they:

  1. Remove themselves (unfunction)
  2. Initialize the real tool
  3. Forward the call

For nvs and SDKMAN, same pattern:

# Lazy nvs
export NVS_HOME="$HOME/.nvs"
export PATH="$NVS_HOME/default/bin:$PATH"  # Default node available immediately

nvs() {
  unfunction nvs 2>/dev/null
  [ -s "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh" ] && . "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh"
  nvs "$@"
}

# Lazy SDKMAN
export SDKMAN_DIR="$HOME/.sdkman"

_sdk_init() {
  unfunction sdk java javac gradle kotlin kotlinc 2>/dev/null
  [[ -s "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh" ]] && source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"
}

sdk() { _sdk_init; sdk "$@" }
java() { _sdk_init; java "$@" }
javac() { _sdk_init; javac "$@" }
gradle() { _sdk_init; gradle "$@" }

Key insight for nvs: Add the default node to PATH directly ($NVS_HOME/default/bin). This way node and npm work instantly without loading nvs. Only nvs use triggers full initialization.

Background the greeting

My shell displayed an inspirational quote on startup. Nice, but blocking.

# Before - blocking
[[ -o interactive ]] && ~/.local/bin/greet

# After - non-blocking
[[ -o interactive ]] && { ~/.local/bin/greet & }

The & backgrounds the process. The quote appears after the prompt is ready.

Consolidating Redundant Tools

While auditing, I found duplicate tools:

InstalledAlso installedResolution
tmuxWezterm (has multiplexer)Removed tmux
htopbtopRemoved htop
treeeza --treeRemoved tree
jenvSDKMANRemoved jenv
brew nodenvsRemoved brew node
iTerm2WeztermRemoved iTerm2
BartenderIce (OSS)Removed Bartender

This freed ~440MB and simplified the mental model.

Wezterm vs tmux

Both provide:

  • Split panes
  • Multiple tabs/windows
  • Session persistence
  • Vim-style navigation

Wezterm advantages:

  • GPU-accelerated rendering
  • Lua config (same language as Neovim)
  • Native macOS integration
  • Built-in smart-splits with Neovim

I kept .tmux.conf for SSH into Linux servers, but local development uses Wezterm exclusively.

The Result

$ time zsh -i -c exit
zsh -i -c exit  0.14s user 0.19s system 68% cpu 0.470 total

2.5s → 0.47s (5.3x faster)

First python call adds ~300ms one time. Worth it.

Full .zshrc Structure

# 1. Oh My Zsh (minimal plugins)
plugins=(git)
source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh

# 2. Environment variables (no subshells)
export EDITOR='nvim'
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
# ... other exports

# 3. Lazy-loaded version managers
# pyenv, nvs, sdkman, gcloud (see above)

# 4. Fast tool initialization
eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"    # ~10ms
eval "$(direnv hook zsh)"    # ~10ms
eval "$(starship init zsh)"  # ~20ms

# 5. Aliases and functions
alias ls="eza --icons"
alias cat="bat"
# ...

# 6. Interactive-only (backgrounded)
[[ -o interactive ]] && { ~/.local/bin/greet & }

Takeaways

  1. Measure first: time zsh -i -c exit before optimizing
  2. Lazy load: If you don't use it every session, defer it
  3. Audit dependencies: Version managers accumulate
  4. Consolidate tools: One multiplexer, one file manager, one top replacement
  5. Background nice-to-haves: Quotes, weather, etc.

The best shell is one you don't notice.

Tools mentioned: Wezterm, Starship, eza, bat, zoxide, Ice

entry.title: Network-Aware Minecraft Server on macOS
entry.summary: I wanted my Minecraft server to automatically start when I connect to my home WiFi, gracefully shut down when I leave, and perform daily maintenance restarts like production game servers. Here's how I set it up on macOS.
entry.content:
I wanted my Minecraft server to automatically start when I connect to my home WiFi, gracefully shut down when I leave, and perform daily maintenance restarts like production game servers. Here's how I set it up on macOS.

The Problem

Running a Minecraft server 24/7 on a laptop isn't practical. I wanted it to:

  • Auto-start when connected to my home network ("HomeWiFi")
  • Gracefully save and stop when disconnecting
  • Restart daily with player warnings (like real game servers)
  • Clean up old logs and crash reports automatically
  • Work without manual intervention

The Solution

A shell script (mc-server-manager) with LaunchAgents for network monitoring and scheduled restarts.

WiFi Detection Gotcha

The commonly recommended approach:

networksetup -getairportnetwork en0

Returns "not associated" on 6GHz WiFi networks, even when connected. This is a known bug on newer macOS versions with WiFi 6E.

The fix is to use system_profiler instead:

system_profiler SPAirPortDataType | \
    awk '/Current Network Information:/{getline; gsub(/^[[:space:]]+|:$/,""); print; exit}'

This correctly returns the SSID regardless of which band you're connected to.

Configuration

All settings live in ~/.config/mc-server/config:

# Network
TARGET_SSID="HomeWiFi"

# Server
SERVER_DIR="$HOME/Development/minecraft/minecraft-server/server"
SESSION_NAME="minecraft-server"

# JVM Memory
MIN_RAM="4G"
MAX_RAM="4G"

# Scheduled restart (24h format, local time)
RESTART_ENABLED="true"
RESTART_HOUR="00"
RESTART_MINUTE="00"
RESTART_TIMEZONE="America/Los_Angeles"

# Warning intervals before restart (seconds)
RESTART_WARNINGS="300 60 30 10 5"

JVM Optimization

The script uses modern Aikar's flags optimized for Paper 1.20+ on Java 21:

build_jvm_flags() {
    local flags=(
        "-Xms${MIN_RAM}" "-Xmx${MAX_RAM}"

        # G1GC optimized for Minecraft's allocation patterns
        "-XX:+UseG1GC"
        "-XX:+ParallelRefProcEnabled"
        "-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200"
        "-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions"
        "-XX:+DisableExplicitGC"
        "-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch"

        # G1GC region sizing
        "-XX:G1NewSizePercent=30"
        "-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=40"
        "-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8M"
        "-XX:G1ReservePercent=20"
        "-XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5"
        "-XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget=4"

        # G1GC tuning
        "-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=15"
        "-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=90"
        "-XX:G1RSetUpdatingPauseTimePercent=5"
        "-XX:SurvivorRatio=32"
        "-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=1"
        "-XX:+PerfDisableSharedMem"

        # Debug helpers (no perf impact)
        "-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError"
        "-XX:HeapDumpPath=$DATA_DIR/heapdump.hprof"
    )
    echo "${flags[*]}"
}

Key points:

  • G1GC is ideal for Minecraft's bursty allocation patterns
  • AlwaysPreTouch pre-allocates memory for consistent latency
  • HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError saves a dump for debugging if OOM occurs
  • Match min/max RAM to avoid heap resizing during gameplay

Scheduled Restarts

Like production game servers, the script supports scheduled restarts with player warnings:

restart_server() {
    local reason="${1:-Scheduled maintenance}"

    # Warnings at 5m, 1m, 30s, 10s, 5s
    for secs in 300 60 30 10 5; do
        server_say "[RESTART] Server restarting in $(format_duration $secs) - $reason"
        sleep_until_next_warning
    done

    server_cmd "save-all"
    server_say "[RESTART] Restarting NOW!"
    server_cmd "stop"

    # Wait for graceful shutdown, then cleanup and restart
    cleanup_server
    start_server
}

The cleanup_server function handles maintenance:

  • Removes logs older than 7 days
  • Removes crash reports older than 30 days
  • Clears stale session locks

LaunchAgents

Two LaunchAgents handle automation:

Network Monitor

com.user.minecraft-server-network - Triggers on WiFi changes:

<key>WatchPaths</key>
<array>
    <string>/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist</string>
    <string>/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/NetworkInterfaces.plist</string>
</array>
<key>StartInterval</key>
<integer>60</integer>

Scheduled Restart

com.user.minecraft-server-restart - Daily at midnight:

<key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
<dict>
    <key>Hour</key>
    <integer>0</integer>
    <key>Minute</key>
    <integer>0</integer>
</dict>

Usage

mc-server-manager status    # Show server state, network, config
mc-server-manager start     # Start server
mc-server-manager stop      # Graceful stop with save
mc-server-manager restart   # Full restart with 5m/1m/30s/10s/5s warnings
mc-server-manager quick     # Quick restart (10s warning)
mc-server-manager attach    # Attach to console (Ctrl+B,D to detach)
mc-server-manager config    # Print current config
mc-server-manager cleanup   # Run maintenance manually
mc-server-manager logs      # Tail manager log

Example output from status:

=== Minecraft Server ===
Server running: yes
Network: HomeWiFi (target: HomeWiFi)
Session: minecraft-server
Attach: tmux attach -t minecraft-server

=== Scheduled Restart ===
Enabled: true
Time: 00:00 (America/Los_Angeles)
Warnings: 300 60 30 10 5

=== Config ===
File: ~/.config/mc-server/config
JVM: 4G - 4G

Why tmux over screen?

macOS ships with screen 4.00.03 from 2006. It lacks features like -Logfile and has quirks with detached sessions. tmux is actively maintained, has better scripting support, and integrates well with the rest of my workflow.

Files

FilePurpose
~/.local/bin/mc-server-managerManagement script (v1.1.0)
~/.config/mc-server/configConfiguration
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-network.plistNetwork monitor
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-restart.plistScheduled restart
~/.local/share/minecraft-server/manager.logManager logs
~/.local/share/minecraft-server/heapdump.hprofOOM heap dump (if triggered)

Setup

# Load the agents
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-network.plist
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-restart.plist

# Generate a config file
mc-server-manager config > ~/.config/mc-server/config

# Edit to taste
vim ~/.config/mc-server/config

Now the server manages itself: starts on home WiFi, stops when leaving, restarts nightly with cleanup, and warns players before any restart.
